newsitem.title: SPAIN: New Bosnia envoy faces uphill battle.
newsitem.headline: New Bosnia envoy faces uphill battle.

text.p: Carlos Westendorp looks more like a dishevelled professor than the no-holds-barred negotiator many believe is needed to revive the stalled peace process in Bosnia.

But supporters say the former Spanish U.N. ambassador, who formally assumes the position of international envoy to Bosnia on Friday, has a 30-year record of diplomatic achievement to prove he is up to the job.
And many believe his close relationship to another key player in the region, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, could mean the difference between success and failure.
Both men were Socialist government foreign ministers in Spain, Westendorp only briefly, and were part of Spain's eight-year battle to join the European Community.

"While it's true that he doesn't have experience in the region he now finds himself in...he knows how to operate at a negotiating table extremely well," said Luis Yanez, a colleague in the former Socialist government. "Westendorp has enormous experience and is brilliant from the diplomatic point of view."

Nevertheless, some critics say Westendorp is a political lightweight whose lack of experience in Bosnia could exacerbate tensions among the former warring factions as the clock ticks down for the withdrawal of 30,000 NATO-led troops next June.
"This is not the time to send in the second string. There is no time for a learning curve," one international official in Bosnia told the Los Angeles Times last month.
Described by peers as intelligent, jovial, hard-working and full of integrity, Westendorp has been handed a difficult task.
He follows former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, who served 18 months as High Representative to Bosnia overseeing the civilian side of the Dayton peace agreement.

Diplomats say the new High Representative takes over against a backdrop of political paralysis in the central government and persistent attempts by indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic to obstruct the Dayton accords.
Bildt, who had trouble building international consensus on Bosnia, warned as he left that war could erupt again unless indicted war criminals were brought to justice and NATO extended its mandate.

On his first day of work on Thursday, Westendorp pushed for the arrest of war criminals as he met members of the collective presidency in the capital Sarajevo and the president of the country's Serb entity, Biljana Plavsic, in Banja Luka.

"They already know what the international community's position is and it's up to the parties involved," Westendorp told Spanish television in Banja Luka. "The parties know perfectly well that until this (war crimes) issue is resolved it will be very difficult to have a situation of normality."

Diplomats see the next couple of months as particularly crucial because of complicated talks on upcoming municipal elections as well as other negotiations to change laws that would enable Bosnia to function as a country.

Westendorp admits he has a big task ahead of him. At 60, he is newly remarried and had hoped to spend more time with his young second family but said he could not shy away from what was "really a challenge".
Commentators in Spain say he is a master of delicate diplomacy.

"He's a bit of a dandy with a tendency to be self-conscious about his roly-poly shape, a characteristic that does not fit with the stiff, haughty image of the classic diplomat," Spanish daily newspaper El Mundo said after his appointment.
"This given, this wandering Madrid native dominates the ins and outs of a negotiation like no one else."

Born in Madrid, Westerndorp earned a law degree and started in Spain's foreign service in 1964. He worked predominantly in European affairs in Madrid and in Brussels, where he was usually on the front line of the main European Union events.
He served as foreign minister for about six months, from December 1995 to May 1996 and was named Spain's chief U.N. representative a year ago.
